en: I take refuge in You alone, Viṣṇu— the supreme, beginningless, and singular one who is established in manifold ways within the secret caves of the primordial nature (prakṛti), the abode of all, and that which dwells within all things moving and unmoving.
Although the entire world is submerged in the ocean of the self, it neither drinks from nor beholds it;
how wondrous that it falsely delights in the ocean of existence, which is like a mirage!
Beholding the world submerged in the ocean of birth, old age, death, and separation arising from dwelling within the womb, the disciple spoke to the Guru with palms joined in reverence.
O Blessed One, you are a knower of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, a destroyer of the multitude of doubts, and a speaker of truth;
I ask you this question concerning the crossing of the ocean of saṃsāra.
In this long cycle of existence, as one wanders, who has what connection with whom?
Who here experiences through comings and goings the karma that yields both auspicious and inauspicious fruits?
Bound by the net of the qualities of karma, the living being transmigrates like a silkworm;
how can there be liberation from its bonds out of the dense darkness of delusion?
"For one who knows the distinction between the qualities (guṇas) and the person (puruṣa), merit and demerit do not become causes of bondage.
Based on these previously stated words, please explain to me both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
Thus the Blessed One, the Support, was questioned by his disciple; he said to him:
"Listen likewise to this which must be told, though it is exceedingly profound even for the wise."
Having prostrated before Upendra, by whom this unreal world was fashioned from the Root Nature (mūlaprakṛti) as if it were real, I shall declare this essence of the ultimate truth.
From the unmanifest, the cosmic egg arose; from the egg, Brahmā; and from him, the creation of beings.
This activity, consisting of illusion, is withdrawn again in due order.
Even though it consists of illusion and is insentient, the collection of qualities and instruments performs actions;
yet the embodied soul, its presiding lord, though possessed of consciousness, does not perform anything at all.
Just as iron, though itself insentient, revolves when in proximity to a magnet,
so too does the aggregate of the organs move within the body presided over by consciousness.
Just as when the sun has risen, this world of living beings performs its activities,
yet the sun neither performs those actions nor causes them to be performed, so too is the Self.
In this world, for the deluded mind— which is stupefied by egoism yet awakened by consciousness— there arises the conceit of being a person, along with the mental construction of pleasure and pain.
"I am the doer, the enjoyer, and the witness of actions such as the highest and so forth"—
thus does the self, though all-pervading and pure by nature, falsely imagine itself.
Just as a pure crystal assumes the color of various objects,
so too does the omnipresent Lord assume the state of that which is colored by the qualities of limiting adjuncts.
As the reflection of the sun moves when the water moves and remains still when it is still,
so too does the self move here when the internal organ moves.
Just as Rāhu, though invisible, becomes manifest in the world when situated within the orb of the moon,
so too the Self, although omnipresent, comes into view when residing in the intellect.
O disciple, that Brahman which is all-pervading, incomparable, non-dual, and accessible to the mind, and which is perceived when it has entered the intellect— that is what must be understood.
Intellect, mind, ego, the groups of subtle elements and senses, and the group of gross elements—
all these products of primordial nature (prakṛti), which are capable of sustaining the creation and preservation of the cycle of worldly existence, are to be abandoned.
In the ultimate sense, merit and demerit, the conceptualization of pleasure and pain, dwelling in heaven or hell,
birth, death, caste, and stage of life do not exist here.
Water in a mirage, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, a serpent in a rope,
and like the double moon seen by one with cataracts— so is the entire form of the world delusory.
Just as the one sun shines in all reservoirs of water,
so does the Supreme Self shine, abiding within all limiting adjuncts.
Like space, Brahman exists within and without all objects, such as jars;
yet the notion of "I" in the body, which is not the Self, leads to the bondage of saṃsāra.
Devoid of all conceptual constructions, pure, awakened, ageless, immortal, and peaceful;
stainless, manifesting all at once, the conscious Self is all-pervading like space.
Just as juice, molasses, sugar, jaggery, and candied sugar are various transformations of the sugarcane,
so too are the diverse states within the Supreme Self itself manifold in form.
Consciousness, the inner controller, the vital breath, the cosmic body (Virāj), birth, and the physical aggregate—
these worldly designations are merely specific states within his own self.
There is no snake in the rope; by what cause does the fear of a snake arise?
Likewise, the delusion of dualistic conceptualization is ignorance; this is not reality.
This is that darkness which consists in the delusion of selfhood in what is not the self;
through it, deluded men do not know Vāsudeva, the soul of all.
Having spread himself out like a net through infinite divisions such as the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth,
Vāsudeva withdraws [it] by means of his own sovereign power, as if playing.

The Fourth (turya) is concealed by those very three— Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña— which are designated as beginning, middle, and end, and which consist of the delusions of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The Lord, as it were, deludes himself by means of his own māyā in the form of duality;
thus he himself perceives the Puruṣa, the Self, who has entered the cave.
Just as various forms appear in the sky through the rising of smoke from a fire,
so too does creation, expanded into duality, appear within Viṣṇu by means of his own māyā.

When the mind is tranquil, he is as if tranquil; when it is joyful, he is as if joyful; when it is deluded, he is as if deluded. While engaged in worldly affairs, he does not, however, become a lord in the ultimate sense.
Just as the expanse of the sky is not soiled by the rising of smoke from small clouds,
even so the Supreme Puruṣa remains untouched by the modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Just as when even a single jar is covered with soot and other impurities, the remaining jars do not become possessed of that impurity, so it is here with the living being (jīva).
The qualities (guṇas) residing in the body and senses perform actions for the sake of their own experience;
for one who knows "I am not the doer, nor is anything mine," action does not bind at all.
The karma performed by means of another body, by which this present body was produced, must necessarily be experienced; its exhaustion is taught to occur only through experience.
That karma accumulated prior to the arising of knowledge, once licked by the crest of the flame of knowledge,
becomes incapable of producing rebirth, like a seed consumed by fire.
Even that action which is performed after the arising of knowledge does not adhere to the agent,
just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
The Buddhas have declared that here in this world, the accumulation of karma is performed through speech, body, and mind;
yet I am not even one among these, nor do I perform those actions.
Through the destruction of the seeds of karma and its fruit, there is the destruction of birth; of this there is no doubt.
Having realized this, one who is free from darkness shines like the sun, possessing the nature of light.
Just as the down of a reed-stalk, when blown by the wind, goes in all ten directions,
so too do the actions of one who knows reality vanish into Brahman through the knowledge of reality.
Just as clarified butter extracted from milk is no longer the same once it has been cast back into it,
so too the conscious self, when separated from the qualities of primordial nature, is not [identical with] that nature.
Having shaken off the dense thicket of illusion consisting of the qualities (guṇas), just as the thousand-rayed sun dispels darkness,
the Puruṣa becomes like a solid mass of salt, moving both externally and internally.
Just as the body and its limbs are merely transformations of clay,
so too the world of the stationary and the moving is non-dual, yet appears as if dual.
From a single Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), many species of Knowers of the Field have arisen,
like clusters of sparks flying in all directions from a fire within iron.
Bound as it were by their own husks due to the fault of association with qualities,
these various kinds of grain obtain birth only so long as they have not been consumed by the fire of knowledge.

While the Self, consisting of pure consciousness, is omnipresent, established as the substratum of all, and composed of the three qualities, ignorance effects creation; yet the Self is not touched by that [ignorance] anywhere.
Just as the causes for the appearance and disappearance of a snake in a rope do not exist,
so too there is no cause here for the arising and destruction of the world.
Free from birth, destruction, going, coming, and the taints of worldly connection, it is eternal;
like space within jars and other vessels, it is the Self of all and is ever-present everywhere.
The association of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) with the fruits of good and evil karma— namely, pleasure and pain—
occurs through that contact, resulting in bondage, just as a non-thief becomes implicated by association with a thief.
As long as the Puruṣa here possesses existence through attachment to the body, qualities, organs, and their objects,
so long does he appear as if bound by the snares of Māyā in saṃsāra.
Deluded by the distinctions of mother, father, son, kinsmen, wealth, and enjoyments,
a living being wanders like a wheel in this world consisting of birth, old age, and death.
Those fools who here worship ignorance, which creates worldly conventions, undergo the nature of birth and death; having entered blind darkness, they suffer.
Just as foam and bubbles are to water, and smoke is to fire,
so too is this Māyā said to be the inherent nature of Viṣṇu.
Thus, having cast aside this delusive Māyā— which consists of the nature of error and the conceptualization of duality—
one should meditate upon Brahman as non-dual, both with and without parts.
Just as water in water, milk in milk, or wind in wind [becomes one],
so too does one attain identity with the stainless Brahman through meditative cultivation.
Thus, when the entire collection of duality has attained the state of Brahman through contemplation,
what delusion and what sorrow can there be for one who perceives everything as Brahman?
Just as a crystal free from impurities shines with its own radiance,
so too does the lamp of consciousness shine here in this world with its own radiance when it is free from limiting adjuncts.

Untouched by the collection of qualities, the instruments, the body, and the vital breaths, as well as by the subtle elements, the classes [of beings], pleasure, and pain— this pervasive one, whose nature is consciousness, is eternally pure.
The embodied self is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the toucher, the taster, and the grasper; yet, being devoid of body, senses, and intellect, it is not the agent.
I am one, yet I do not abide in any single place; through the possession of sovereignty, I pervade this entire universe like space—of this there is no doubt whatsoever.
When one contemplates that all this— both the partless and the with-parts— is indeed the Self alone, at that very moment,
freed from the thicket of delusion, one becomes the Supreme Goddess.
Whatever those blinded by passion proclaim regarding established doctrines, scriptures, and logic,
we approve of all that with the understanding that it is the doctrine of the Self of All.
In whatever form the Blessed One is worshipped,
assuming that very form, he approaches [the devotee] like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Having known Nārāyaṇa as the Self, who is the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution,
one becomes omniscient, omnipresent, all, and the Lord of all.
The knower of the self crosses over sorrow; since the wise man fears nothing from any quarter, even from death he has no fear of dying—how much less from anything else?
That which is eternally free from decrease and increase, destruction and killing, and bondage and liberation—this is the ultimate reality; everything other than this is false.
Thus, having discerned both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, one who has cast off the web of conceptual constructions,
delighting in the Self and established in tranquility, becomes isolated.
Just as the reeds, lotus stalks, and bamboo perish upon reaching their own flowers,
so too those things that have become one's own nature perish upon attaining that very nature.
When the knot of ignorance is split asunder, when the multitude of doubts is severed,
and when the auspicious seed of birth is consumed and exhausted, one goes to Hari, the Supreme Self.
Liberation has no abode whatsoever, nor does it involve going anywhere else;
they know that liberation to be the breaking of the knot consisting of ignorance.
Having thus understood this unreal form of the world to be composed of Viṣṇu’s māyā,
one should become peaceful, free from attachment to enjoyments characterized by the dualities of the limiting adjuncts.
Having realized that nature is distinct, the person, though situated in the midst of saṃsāra,
becomes liberated from all karmas, just as a lotus leaf is by water.
Whether eating this or that, clothed in whatever manner, tranquil,
and sleeping wherever he may be, one whose self is the soul of all beings is liberated.
Even if one performs millions of horse-sacrifices or commits hundreds of thousands of murders of Brahmins,
the knower of the ultimate truth remains stainless, untouched by either merit or sin.
One whose speech and intellect are free from intoxication, anger, joy, envy, despondency, fear, and harshness;
who is devoid of praise and the *vaṣaṭ* call; and whose mind is unfathomable—such a person should wander like one who is dull-witted.
Having thus realized the ultimate reality, which is devoid of arising and destruction,
one who has accomplished what was to be done and whose birth has become fruitful remains omnipresent, moving according to his will.
He who knows the all-pervading, undivided, and universal self, from which all diversity has been shaken off,
as incomparable supreme bliss, becomes one with that.
Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even if he has lost his memory while casting off the body,
he is liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge and, with his sorrow destroyed, attains absolute isolation.
Visiting sacred fords leads to merit; going to the home of a dog-cooker at the time of death leads to hell.
But when there is no contact with the stain of merit or demerit, what is the use of either?
Just as a man whose foot has slipped from the top of a tree falls to the ground even against his will,
so too one who knows the distinction between the qualities (guṇas) and the person (puruṣa) becomes isolated (kevalin), even though he does not desire it.
Having begun the practice of the path to the ultimate truth, even if he has not yet attained yoga,
one who enjoys the pleasures of the celestial realms rejoices for a long time with a joyful mind.
Just as a sovereign emperor is honored by all people within his realm,
so too is one who has fallen from yoga honored by all the gods throughout the worlds.
After a long time, having attained a great human birth and practiced yoga,
one reaches the divine nectar— that supreme state of Viṣṇu.
Having examined the entire scripture of Vedānta, Śeṣa, the support of the world,
composed this *Paramārthasāra* by means of the *Āryāpañcāśīti*.
Thus ends the Paramārthasāra.
